posts.content:
APRF is a new draft specification specification for mailbox reporting.

Gives you reporting on:
▪️ Classification: where do mailbox providers place your emails?
▪️ Engagement: how do real users interact with your emails?

Here's what you need to know 👇

Classification details whether your emails arrive in the inbox, the spam folder, or other inbox specific folders like the Promotions tab.

Engagement is recorded as positive, negative or neutral.

The spec doesn't define what user actions counts as positive, negative, or neutral, but it does make the following suggestions:

▪️Positive: opening, clicking, or removing from spam
▪️Negative: sending to spam, deleting without opening, unsubscribing
▪️Neutral: forwarding, filing

APRF may be a draft spec, but Comcast is already sending out reports. While no other mailbox supports it yet, Google is a co-author of the spec so we can hope to see it in Gmail in the future.

It also offers more granular reporting per custom segmentations.

APRF is definitely worth watching. Receiving reports of how users engage with your emails directly from the mailbox provider is invaluable for understanding your domain reputation.

posts.content:
Announcing OAuth Client ID Metadata Documents (CIMD)

This new registration method:
▪️ gives clients a stable identity across installations
▪️ reduces per-install registration and cleanup
▪️ supports the new MCP specification

CIMD simplifies building OAuth clients for Resend👇

With CIMD, the client hosts a metadata document that Resend fetches and validates the document during authorization, giving the client one stable identity across installations.

Clients that support only DCR will continue to work, as this change is backwards compatible.

🙋 What can you build with it?

▪️ Remote MCP servers
▪️ Distributed CLIs 
▪️ Public OAuth clients

Here's how it works 👇

1️⃣ Host a JSON document describing your client.

The document's client_id must be the same URL where the document is hosted.

2️⃣ Pass the URL as the client_id in the auth request

Resend fetches the document, validates the client metadata, and runs the rest of the authorization code and PKCE flow.

DCR continues to work for clients that depend on it. If you can host a public JSON document, view our full guide for caching rules, full field references, and redirect URI requirements.

https://lnkd.in/ez4R5EGT

CIMD gives public OAuth clients a stable identity without requiring a separate registration for every installation.

posts.content:
You may soon be able to verify email addresses directly in the browser.

There's a new API proposal that could help verifying your users' email addresses without sending them away from your app to their inbox.

The new proposal keeps the user in control while minimizing friction.

1. The user enter their email address into a form on your site.
2. The browser checks that they have a logged-in session with their mailbox.
3. The subscriber is immediately verified.

The browser does the work to verify.  Three things happen silently:

1.  The browser and mailbox provider add a token to a hidden input
2. Submitting the form submits the token with their email address
3. Server side validation ensures the email address belongs to the user

With this API, you can:

▪️ verify the user owns the email address without leaving the browser.
▪️ gain confidence that an address belongs to the user
▪️ reduce bounces caused by invalid or mistyped addresses

Both of these features help protect your sender reputation.

If your server is written in JavaScript, we built an npm package to perform the verification for you. You can install it with:


You can use it in your code by passing the email, token, audience (your site's origin), and nonce. 

Explore this full Next.js application to see how it all works together. 

https://lnkd.in/eyF56vzF

Or try the example app for yourself.

https://lnkd.in/etjHyUd5

This is an experimental API for now, so it only works in Chrome and has only been implemented by Gmail. It's a good time to experiment with it as a progressive enhancement.

Read the full blog post for more details 👇

🔥 Pro Tip 🔥

Gmail is tightening email requirements. It impacts those sending 5k> emails a day to Gmail servers. 

Since February 1, 2024, Gmail has "required" senders to follow new email sender guidelines. Now, after 2 years, they're starting to enforce it. 

Here's what you need to know 👇

1️⃣ SPF & DKIM authentication

These two DNS records protect you from spoofers pretending to send on your behalf and give inboxes like Gmail more confidence in your emails.

Resend requires these two records for every domain.

https://lnkd.in/ewv9_cPS

 2️⃣ DMARC policy

DMARC is another record that tells mail servers what to do with messages that don't pass SPF or DKIM.

You can set your DMARC policy to none, but Gmail requires those sending >5k/day have a DMARC policy.

https://lnkd.in/dS2DaYi7

3️⃣ Keep spam rates below 0.10%

Resend requires senders stay below 0.08% to help proactively protect your reputation. Tips to keep a spam rate low:

1. Let recipients opt out of emails.
2. Send relevant and timely emails.
3. Get proper email consent.

https://lnkd.in/dCHw6G9S

4️⃣ One-click unsubscribe for marketing

When you send with Broadcasts, Resend can handle unsubscribes automatically.

You can also include the custom header `List-Unsubscribe-Post: List-Unsubscribe=One-Click` to build your own and accept POST requests.

https://lnkd.in/eYeNnzxh

5️⃣ Use TLS connection

You can configure enforced TLS for any domain in Resend.

https://lnkd.in/eZYDjQsG
